title: Cycle Credit System for Role-Level Fairness and Outcome Prioritization
creator: Aisha Thompson
description:
Problem: During cycle planning we repeatedly see role-level contention (senior infra, frontend, applied-ml time) where a few initiatives consume scarce role-hours early and create ripple delays for high-OKR work. Current approaches (percent-based reserves, ad-hoc reassignments, and manual negotiation) are opaque and lead to unbalanced outcomes and morale friction.

Proposal summary: Introduce a "Cycle Credit System" (CCS) that allocates discrete, transferable "focus credits" to initiatives at role granularity (e.g., 120 engineer-hours = 12 dev credits, 40 infra hours = 4 infra credits). Credits are awarded by combining: (1) objective OKR alignment score, (2) delivery risk and maturity, and (3) a scarcity multiplier per role derived from historical utilization. Initiatives spend credits during planning to secure role commitments. Credits are partially refundable for predictable work (e.g., production bug queues), and a small pool of discretionary credits is retained cross-initiative to handle emergent security or oncall work.

Key goals: make trade-offs explicit at time of commitment, reduce last-minute staffing firefights, improve predictability for platform and reliability work, and create a lightweight market that encourages initiatives to reduce wasted scope. The system is intended as a planning-layer experiment for 2 cycles with metrics to evaluate fairness, on-time delivery, and developer satisfaction.
acceptance_criteria: Cycle planner UI mock (console wireframe) showing role-level credit ledger and initiative checkout is reviewed by PM + Eng leads
Allocation algorithm defined: input signals (OKR weight, complexity score, role scarcity) and deterministic credit math documented
Pilot cohort of 8 initiatives from product and platform agree to participate for 2 cycles and sign a light SLA for credit spend transparency
Automated ledger created in Google Sheet (or product console staging) to track credits per initiative and role each cycle
Three metric dashboards defined and instrumented: fairness index, credit spend vs actual hours, and initiative delivery hit-rate
proposed_solution: Implement CCS as a planning-layer service (initially Google Sheet + Ops process) with these components: (1) credit issuance job that runs after intake and OKR scoring, (2) planning checkout where PMs allocate credits per role to stories, (3) weekly reconciliation where leads confirm hours vs credits used, (4) governance: credit appeals channel and small cross-functional review board to adjudicate disputes. Long-term: integrate ledger into Redwood Console cycle-planner feature and surface role-level contention warnings during roadmap edits.
rollout_plan: Week 0: Align exec and Eng leads; finalize scoring rubric and scarcity multipliers
Week 1: Build Google Sheet ledger, create lightweight onboarding doc, and run tabletop with 3 pilot teams
Week 2-3: Pilot first planning cadence; capture qualitative feedback and adjust multipliers
Cycle 1 runtime: Reconcile weekly, collect metrics, and log appeals
Post-pilot: Design Console integration PRD if metrics meet targets and pilot feedback positive
metrics: Fairness index: variance of credit-to-hour ratio across initiatives (target: < 15% by end of pilot)
Delivery hit-rate: percent of pilot initiatives that meet committed scope within allocated credits (target: 70%+)
Role churn: percent of role reassignments due to contention mid-cycle (target: reduce by 40%)
Developer sentiment: pulse survey delta on planning fairness (target: +0.5 on 5-point scale)
Cost of overhead: additional hours spent in planning to manage credits (target: < 3% of cycle effort)
risks: Gaming the system: teams may underreport complexity to get more credits; mitigated by peer review and post-cycle reconciliation
Process overhead could outweigh benefit if ledger requires heavy manual bookkeeping; mitigated by strict scope: start with 8 pilots and a simple sheet
Pushback from leaders who prefer absolute control over role assignments; mitigated by framing CCS as experiment and keeping governance lightweight
Credit hoarding: initiatives may hoard credits to hedge uncertainty; mitigate via partial expiration and explicit refund rules
notes: Design idea inspired by capacity marketplaces used in consulting firms and internal 'oncall token' experiments in infra teams.
If pilot succeeds, propose a follow-up PRD to embed CCS into console roadmap editor with visual warnings when scarce roles exceed 70% commit for a cycle.
Owner: PM Guild sponsoring experiment; Eng leads for infra, platform, and frontend to co-sign initial multipliers.
